cautions: Do not conclude the GPU is dead from XID 79 alone — thermal trips and power droop present identically.
Do not reboot and return the node to the pool without the Redfish check; the fault will recur under load.
steps: Confirm the event: grep dmesg for 'Xid 79' and note GPU PCI address, node, and timestamp.
Check Redfish out-of-band telemetry: inlet temperature, GPU hotspot if reported, and PSU redundancy status.
If PSU redundancy is lost or PCIe uncorrectable counters are above zero, treat power delivery as the prime suspect and check input draw vs provisioned capacity before touching the card.
If hotspot is high while inlet is normal (roughly 23-27C), suspect card cooling (heatsink mount, fan zone) rather than the room.
Drain the node so no new work lands on it while diagnosis continues.
If power and thermal look normal, reseat or move the card; if XID 79 persists after reseat, open an RMA/service ticket.
summary: The driver lost PCIe communication with the GPU. In this project's triage experience the cause is more often power delivery or a thermal trip than a dead card, so evidence comes first: in-band tools cannot see the card in this state, which makes out-of-band Redfish telemetry the primary source.
symptoms: node lost a gpu under load
title: XID 79 — GPU has fallen off the bus

cautions: Do not simply reboot and return the node to the pool — uncorrectable errors tend to recur.
A single XID 48 is drain-and-watch; recurrence, not the first event, is the RMA trigger in this runbook.
evidence_to_collect: prior XID 92 history for the same GPU
steps: Drain the node so no new work lands on the affected GPU.
Keep the GPU idle and record the event with GPU serial, slot, and node for the service record.
Check whether the same GPU reported XID 92 (single-bit ECC storm) in the preceding days — that is the classic precursor pattern.
If the same GPU reports XID 48 again within 24 hours, treat the card as degraded and open an RMA/service ticket per site policy.
summary: The GPU's DRAM reported an error ECC could not correct; the affected memory region is unreliable. This is a hardware-trust problem, not an application problem.
title: XID 48 — Double-bit ECC error (uncorrectable)

cautions: Do not drain on a single isolated XID 92 — correctable errors are expected background noise at fleet scale.
Do not ignore a sustained storm either; that is exactly how an XID 48 surprises you later.
steps: Note the GPU and start watching its ECC counters (nvidia-smi -q) on a short cadence.
Track the XID 92 rate over time; a rising trend matters more than any single count.
If XID 92 keeps firing at a sustained rate, or XID 48 appears on the same GPU, drain the node and escalate.
summary: Single-bit errors are correctable, so nothing is broken yet — but a rising SBE rate is the early-warning signal that often precedes uncorrectable double-bit errors (XID 48). The correct response is watchful monitoring, not panic and not silence.
title: XID 92 — Excessive single-bit ECC interrupts

cautions: Do not RMA a single card for XID 74 before checking whether neighbors report it too.
Do not return a node to the pool while the link is still training dirty.
steps: Check for correlated XID 74 events on neighbor GPUs in the same window.
Check the NVLink bridges/switch for the platform per vendor documentation.
Correlate with Redfish PCIe/fabric error counters if available.
Drain affected nodes and do not return them until the link trains cleanly again.
summary: An error on the NVLink fabric between GPUs. The key diagnostic move is correlation: clustered XID 74 events on neighbor GPUs point at the fabric or switch, not at one card.
title: XID 74 — NVLink error

cautions: Do not loop resets indefinitely; one reset, then drain-and-escalate on recurrence.
steps: Attempt a GPU reset (nvidia-smi --gpu-reset) where the platform supports it.
Verify the GPU returns and trains cleanly after reset.
If GSP errors repeat on the same GPU after reset, drain the node and escalate — recurring GSP faults usually end in a service ticket.
summary: The GPU System Processor — the GPU's embedded microcontroller — stopped responding to the driver. Reset is the first response; recurrence after reset is the escalation signal.
title: XID 119/120 — GSP RPC timeout / GSP error

cautions: Do not drain the node on a single XID 13 or 31 — that trades a software bug for lost fleet capacity.
Do not dismiss a cross-workload pattern on one GPU as 'just the app' either.
steps: Check the application first: recent code or deploy change, bad input batch, out-of-bounds access patterns.
Check whether the same workload fails on a different, known-good GPU (moves with the job = software; stays with the GPU = hardware).
Escalate to hardware triage only if the same GPU throws XID 13/31 across unrelated workloads.
summary: Usually application-level: an illegal memory access by the CUDA workload rather than broken hardware. The discipline in this runbook is restraint — a single occurrence is a software conversation, not a node drain.
title: XID 13 / 31 — Graphics Engine Exception / GPU memory page fault

cautions: Do not treat XID 63 as a fault — it is the hardware working as designed.
Do not keep resetting a GPU whose PMU halts repeatedly.
steps: Identify which code fired; the response differs per code, not per 'memory-ish' feeling.
XID 62: GPU reset; if the PMU keeps halting after reset, drain and escalate instead of resetting in a loop.
XID 63: log it and watch the single-bit error trend; no other action.
XID 64: GPU reset; drain and escalate on recurrence, treating it as a hardware memory problem.
summary: Three related codes with three different postures. XID 62 (PMU halt): reset first, escalate on recurrence. XID 63 (row retirement): informational — the GPU is containing ECC errors by remapping as designed, note the SBE trend only. XID 64 (retirement failure): containment failed — reset, then drain and escalate if it recurs.
title: XID 62 / 63 / 64 — PMU halt and DRAM row retirement

cautions: Do not page anyone for XID 45 alone.
Do not let a chained XID 45 hide the real error next to it.
evidence_to_collect: co-occurring XID codes in the same window
steps: Log the event and move on.
Investigate only if XID 45 appears chained with real error XIDs (for example 48 or 79) in the same time window — then follow the other code's runbook.
summary: The benign XID: the user application was aborted (Ctrl-C, GPU reset, sigkill) and the driver tore down the GPU context. This is cleanup, not a fault.
title: XID 45 — Preemptive removal after application abort (benign)

cautions: Never interpret a hotspot number without the inlet number next to it; the comparison is the diagnosis.
steps: Hotspot above roughly 85C with a normal inlet (23-27C) points at the card's cooling: heatsink mount, fan zone, thermal interface.
Hotspot high AND inlet high points at facility cooling instead.
PSU redundancy lost (psu_redundancy_ok=false) alongside XID 79: check input power draw vs provisioned capacity before touching the card.
PCIe uncorrectable error counters above zero in Redfish, alongside XID 79 or 74, strengthen the case for a bus/fabric problem.
Always correlate thermal alerts with XID 79 before concluding a GPU is dead — many 'fallen off the bus' events are thermal trips in disguise.
summary: How this project reads Redfish BMC telemetry when in-band tools are blind or ambiguous. Thermal: compare GPU hotspot against chassis inlet. Power: PSU redundancy lost plus XID 79 is the classic signature of a power-delivery problem, not a dead GPU.
title: Redfish out-of-band interpretation — thermal and power

cautions: Never invent a meaning or a remediation for an unknown XID code.
Single isolated events, especially XID 13/31, are usually noise; do not escalate noise.
evidence_to_collect: raw dmesg line for unknown codes
steps: For any event, first count occurrences of the same code on the same GPU in the last 24 hours and apply the one-level upgrade if it repeats.
For an unknown XID code: mark severity unknown, route to human review, and record the raw dmesg line so the code can be researched against vendor documentation.
An unknown code with a healthy Redfish profile is usually a new firmware event, not an emergency — but it still goes to a human, not to a guess.
summary: Two rules that govern every other runbook in this set. Repeat rule: the same XID code on the same GPU twice within 24 hours upgrades the response one level (check becomes drain, drain becomes drain plus escalate) — recurrence is the signal that separates a flaky card from a bad run. Unknown rule: a code that is not in the lookup table is never guessed at.
symptoms: same xid twice in one day
title: Meta-rules — repeat events and unknown XID codes
